title: How the Blue LED Was Invented
subtitle: Three decades, three researchers, one stubborn crystal

slides.title: How the Blue LED Was Invented
slides.subtitle: Three decades, three researchers, one stubborn crystal
slides.author: Materials Science & Technology
slides.notes: Open with the hook: red and green LEDs existed by the late 1960s. Blue took until 1993, and it is the one that made white light possible. Everything that follows is about why the last colour was the hard one.

slides.title: The Colour That Wouldn't Come
slides.text: Red arrived in 1962. Blue stayed dark for three more decades.
slides.notes: Set the scale of the problem: this was not a detail left to polish, it was a wall the whole field hit.

slides.title: Light colour is set by the band gap
bullets: A light-emitting diode works when an electron drops across a semiconductor's **band gap** and releases the energy as a photon.
**Red** photons need about **1.9 eV**. **Blue** photons need about **2.7 eV** — a much wider gap.
Wide-gap semiconductors are the hardest to grow, the hardest to dope, and the hardest to make electrical contact to.
So the physics did not make blue impossible. It made it **everything that is difficult, at once**.
slides.source: Nobel Prize in Physics 2014, information for the public
slides.notes: Keep the physics to one sentence: photon energy equals band gap. The point is that a wider gap forces you into materials the semiconductor industry had no idea how to handle.

slides.title: Six dates that tell the story

items.label: Round
items.text: A faint glow from silicon carbide — the first electroluminescence, and unusable.

items.label: RCA
items.text: Pankove builds the first GaN light emitter. Orders of magnitude too dim.

items.label: Nagoya
items.text: Amano and Akasaki grow the first usable GaN crystal.

items.label: Nagoya
items.text: The same team makes GaN p-type. A working junction becomes possible.

items.label: Nichia
items.text: Nakamura ships a high-brightness blue LED.

items.label: Nobel
items.text: Akasaki, Amano and Nakamura share the Prize in Physics.

slides.source: Nobel Prize in Physics 2014; IEEE Milestone, 1989-1993
slides.notes: This is the roadmap for the rest of the deck. Note the 86-year span between the first glimmer and a marketable lamp.

slides.title: Why GaN was written off

left.heading: The problems nobody had solved
bullets: No usable GaN crystal — films cracked on every available substrate.
No p-type GaN — so no junction, and without a junction there is no diode.
Devices that did emit were orders of magnitude too dim to sell.

right.heading: Where the field went instead
bullets: Zinc selenide looked easier, so most groups followed it.
GaN was widely treated as a dead end.
The Nobel citation's own framing: they "succeeded where everyone else had failed."

slides.source: Nobel Prize in Physics 2014, press release
slides.notes: The interesting part of this story is a research-culture lesson: a field converging on the wrong material because the right one was harder to grow. Worth a pause.

slides.title: Breaking the Crystal Barrier
slides.text: Three problems, solved in order, by two groups years apart.
slides.notes: Transition from the problem to the solution. Clock: the three fixes are 1986, 1989 and 1993.

slides.title: Three blockers, and what broke each one
rows: GaN films cracked and came out unusable
Mg-doped GaN stayed insulating; without a p-side there is no junction
Early GaN emitters were orders of magnitude too dim
slides.source: Amano et al., Jpn. J. Appl. Phys. 28 (1989); Nakamura et al., Appl. Phys. Lett. 64 (1994)
slides.notes: Emphasise that these had to happen in order. The buffer layer made a crystal good enough that doping experiments meant anything; p-type made a junction; the double heterostructure made the junction bright.

slides.title: A Working Light
slides.text: What the 1993 diode actually does, and why it changed lighting.
slides.notes: Shift from invention history to the device itself and its consequences.

slides.title: How the blue LED makes light

items.label: InGaN active layer
items.note: Electrons and holes recombine here, emitting a blue photon

items.label: Sapphire substrate
items.note: The lattice-mismatched base the whole stack is grown on

slides.notes: The active layer is the whole trick: a thin InGaN layer between a p-side and an n-side. The indium content sets the wavelength, which is also why the same structure tuned to more indium gives green.

slides.title: One number explains the Nobel Prize
bullets: A filament bulb turns most of its power into heat: **16 lm/W**.
The best white LED passed **300 lm/W** by 2014.
Lighting was about **one quarter** of world electricity consumption.
slides.source: Nobel Prize in Physics 2014, press release
slides.notes: Read the ratio aloud: roughly 19 times the useful light per watt. That is the energy argument the prize cited, and it is the whole reason a physics prize went to a light fitting.

slides.title: What blue made possible
headers: Why it had to be blue
rows: A blue LED pumps a yellow phosphor; blue plus yellow reads as white
A blue-violet laser focuses to a smaller spot, so more data fits on a disc
Red and green diodes already existed; blue completed the three-colour gamut
slides.notes: The phosphor trick is the answer to 'why did they need blue for white light?' — you cannot make white by adding red to green. You need the short-wavelength end.

slides.title: Why it won the Nobel Prize
slides.text: for the invention of efficient blue light-emitting diodes which has enabled bright and energy-saving white light sources
slides.attribution: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, 7 October 2014
slides.notes: The citation is deliberately about the enabling, not the diode. The Academy rewarded the consequence, not just the component.
